We made Backplane to actually use Fable, Astra, etc. as real electrical engineers! It incorporates KiCad + your favorite harness (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Grok) to accelerate hardware development. You can use it "autonomously" or work alongside the agent, making changes or comments to redirect the agent as it works. Also has some slick skills for schematic editing, BOM management.

Hardware is in its "tab to accept changes"/copilot era rather than its agentic era imo.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, my team just released box by Simular, a cloud computer for all your agents, with fast computer use built-in.

box gives your agents one remote Ubuntu desktop with Chrome and a shell, which your AI can then drive over MCP while your own computer stays unoccupied.

That means you can turn your basic ChatGPT plan into a personal agent by giving it a box computer; let your Claude Code pick up what Codex has left off on the same box to maximize usage; actually close your laptop and let tasks run in one persistent, 24/7 environment with all your logins and setup.

Some box demos: https://x.com/SimularAI/status/2121329778896871665?a=U4U1yYT...

We started on this because we believe computers shouldn't need human operation in the future. When agents arrived, people started running them on mini computers and you see colleagues walk around the office with their laptop lid open. We think there's a better solution - cloud computers engineered for agents.

Simular started three years ago to build out the full stack of an autonomous computer. box is our attempt to give agents a body to live in.

Our computer use outperformed Opus and GPT on OSWorld, costing fewer tokens. https://thenewstack.io/sai-agent-osworld-benchmark/

Copy/paste one command into your agent to start:

"Set up box from https://box.simular.ai/install"

You can watch box's live action from a dashboard https://box.simular.ai/box

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback. I'll be in comments here to answer any question.

story_text.value:
View runs small rust programs as native interfaces using Rust and GPUI. Coding agents write and edit the programs. Changes load without restarting the app.

Each view has its own state and permissions. Views access data through APIs, CLIs or MCP servers.

It supports Pi, Codex, Claude Code and OpenCode and more. Saved state is encrypted locally. Credentials are stored in macOS Keychain.

story_text.value:
hi HN, I'm AJ.

Have been using Claude Code every day, and I was done re-typing the same project rules in every new chat. So I built this.

We try to follow some rules in our coding projects. For eg: "we use pnpm, not npm". The problem is, i tell claude about this rule in one chat, when i start another chat, i have to retype it. Also, when my team opens the same repo using another ai tool lets say cursor, they dont see the rule in their chat. Not cool.

So I built jevmem. It saves your project's rules in a file in your repo. and before Claude Code runs a command, it checks the command against those rules.

How it works:

1) You chat with Claude Code like normal.

2) jevmem saves your rules, decisions and everything that failed, one line each, in a file called JEVMEM.md in your repo.

3) You commit JEVMEM.md like any other file.

4) Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can all read it. now, your team also gets it when they pull.

for example: on Mon you tell Claude "we use pnpm, not npm". On Tuesday your teammate pulls and opens the repo in Cursor. They can see the pnpm rule.

oh and guard is my favourite part. So before Claude Code runs a command or edits a file, jevmem checks it against your rules. If it may break one of your rules, Claude Code stops and asks you first.

Eg: your rule is "don't hand-edit db/migrations/, those files are generated". 3weeks later, in a new session if claude tries to edit a migration, Claude Code stops and shows:

jevmem: this may break a saved rule: "Don't hand-edit db/migrations/: those files are generated." (JEVMEM.md)

You can also retrieve failed attempt. Like if you tried caching API responses in memory, and it broke the build, claude will remember that and some time later when you do the same thing, Claude tells you "Already tried: ..." with the reason.

Numbers from our tests:

-> Claude broke a project rule and left it in the code: 0 of 15 sessions with jevmem, 9 of 15 without it. We checked each one by hand.

-> Claude followed decisions made earlier in the project: 66 of 72 sessions with jevmem, 28 of 72 without.

Tbh, a CLAUDE.md file that you keep updating yourself did about as well here (67 of 72). The difference is that jevmem updates the file for you, likewise for cursor and codex.

jevmem also works alongside Claude Code's own auto memory. It doesn't replace it.

The catches:

- The guard works in Claude Code only. - You need a paid TypeSafe API key. jevmem's requests are billed to that key. - Your message text is sent to TypeSafe to be scored. Common secrets are removed first. - Nothing stored remotely. You turn it on per project. - We ran the tests on our own test projects.

(MIT license) Full results: https://avinash-jetwani.github.io/jevmem/results/

Install:

1. In claude: Plugins > Discover > jevmem > Add

2. npm install -g jevmem

3. In your project folder: jevmem setup

Repo: https://github.com/Avinash-jetwani/jevmem

I'd like to hear about your genuine feedback and how we could make it better!

title.value: Show HN: Jevmem – Auto Tracked Project Rules for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor

story_text.value:
Hi, I'm Max. I've used many hosts file switchers over the years to do local development with real hostnames/domains, combined with HTTPS reverse-proxies.

I made HostsTray to combine both into one tool.

Through a tray icon (Windows) or menu bar (macOS) you can toggle groups of hosts file entries, and toggle the HTTPS proxy.

The HTTPS proxy first installs a local CA cert into your keychain/certificate store, and then uses it to create certificates for each domain that passes through the proxy.

You can configure the proxy to route different paths to different ports locally. Websockets are also supported.

A common problem when editing hosts file is to make Chrome/other browser actually update the DNS cache. I found this is due to Chrome holding a pool of open connections in the background. HostsTray solves this by dropping the open connections to addresses that changed, forcing Chrome to reconnect and re-lookup the hostnames. It is VERY satisfying to toggle a hosts group and see Chrome obey immediately.

Switching can be password-free using an optional helper that runs as admin. The helper only does switching/toggling of groups you already have.

HostsTray also exposes a local API to toggle hosts groups and the proxy. The API also serves a skill suitable for coding agents. So you can let Claude Code toggle for you. It can also add new hostnames to HostsTray, but that requires user verification from you.

The whole thing is a ~10 MB binary written in Go, open-source for Windows and macOS.

Hope this can be useful Feedback is very welcome.

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Balázs, and I wanted to share my passion project that I've been building in my free time. It is free, it is open-source, and I've poured a lot of love into making it delightful.

I've spent a lot of time dabbling with agentic ADEs and IDEs since the days of the early VSCode forks. I've switched IDEs more times than I can count. Cursor. Copilot. Codex. PearAI. Orca. Claude Code. OpenCode. Superset. Agent Orchestrator. Windsurf, and then Devin. OpenChamber. Kilo. IntelliJ and VSCode plugins.

This September, I felt sort of stranded. I kept switching tools, losing all my chats, losing time, and frankly, losing love for the very thing that has been getting me out of bed every morning for the past decade. Programming. Building. Tinkering. I've spent more time fighting my tools, being forced back into terminals, being rug-pulled by labs, or being forced into the cloud, when really, I just want to work on my machine.

It was then that I started to jot down my frustrations in a blog post. Not that anyone would read it, especially these days, but my frustrations, I felt, needed an outlet. As I was writing the post, I sort of realised: for the longest time, I'd been observing and obsessing over products like Linear. Raycast. Arc. Their level of detail. Their thoughtful approach to UX. Their grassroots, scratch-a-boring-itch story.

So I decided to scratch my itch, and build an IDE that would stay out of your way. It's called Althar. Delightful to use, calm, and open, rethinking the old paradigms that are holding most of the industry captive. There's no sidebar. There's no built-in text editor. There are no chats (in a traditional sense).

Agents forgetting my project between tasks always annoyed me. So did my overarching goals and milestones getting lost between chats, and agents having no way to coordinate work with one another. In most tools I've tried, they work in silos.

So, in Althar, you organise your work in projects. A project can be a single repository, or many. On top of it sits your project manager, called the coordinator. You talk to her like you would talk to any PM on a project. You could say something like, "Help me make my website responsive and accessible. Also, help me measure the performance with Lighthouse." She will then split the work into three separate tasks, brief individual task agents called leads, assign each task a reviewer agent (we love a second opinion, but it's optional), and send them on their way.

Finished work comes back to you with screenshots, test evidence, and the reviewer's findings settled.

You see everything that's happening on a kanban-like board (though it is NOT kanban), and you're only pulled in when you're actually needed. No need to anxiously watch over terminals and in-flight agent thinking trails.

You can use all of your existing subscriptions. Claude. Codex. OpenCode and so on. It connects to your issue trackers and git hosts, wherever they may be.

Work happens locally. Next week, I hope to add support for remote runners, and I'm also working on a mobile companion.

I hope you'll enjoy it. There is so much to say, so many little details. But it's also early days, so please, if you do find issues, let me know :) Or open a pull request. The open source community has given me so much over the years. It is the best thing about software engineering, and something unique to our profession. I'm excited that I get to give back.

title.value: Show HN: Althar – an open-source IDE where agents review each other's work
